$comment: Riftlight authored opening draft. Development preview only; see ../README.md. Production campaign id will be riftlight. No bonus XP: preserve the design bible campaign budget.
title: The River in the Memory Ice

goal.text: Compare your crossing with the yetis' memory ice.

steps.label: Show a newcomer how to look

arrival.narration: An elder yeti welcomes your party at a room cut into the glacier. Small catalog shelves stand beside a broad marked floor. Pip lays the changed-crossing account on a low stone table. The elder listens to the whole report before pointing toward a newly exposed face of ice. "We have looked at that memory three times. We should compare the looks, not hurry the answer." She invites everyone to warm their hands before choosing a place to stand.

variants.text: Your account records how the party crossed by the high rock reach. The elder leaves that checked route separate from the river's older course.
Your account records the supported low-shelf crossing and its withdrawal before the water returned. The elder keeps the crossing sequence beside the memory notes.

quiet_rule.narration: The elder sets a cup of warm tea on a flat stone and waits until every hero is inside the marked waiting space. Beyond it, a pale face of memory ice has been newly uncovered. "Do not shout near the old ice; you do not know what you might wake." She offers no name for what she means. Your party can ask how to work quietly before approaching, rather than testing the warning. What should the room's stop signal be?

choices.label: Agree on a raised hand that everyone can see
Agree that any friend may quietly call a pause
Let a songkeeper lead a quiet pause signal

quiet_rule_1.narration: You practice the signal while still beside the warm cup. Pip stands where he can see the whole group. Each hero repeats the stop before lowering a hand. The elder checks the places from which a small friend might be hidden behind a larger one.

quiet_rule_1_check.prompt: Agree on a raised hand that everyone can see. Choose who leads while the others help.

quiet_rule_1_done.narration: The whole group stops at the first signal, including Pip. The elder nods once and moves the cup away from the walking lane. You have a room rule everyone can use before there is anything surprising to look at.

quiet_rule_1_changed.narration: One friend cannot see the signal or hear the first quiet word. You change where the group stands and try the instruction facing one another. Everyone can repeat it before the elder leads you forward. Nothing in the old ice is tested by a shout.

quiet_rule_2.narration: You choose one short word and practice it at speaking level. The elder shows how a low voice carries across the floor without shouting. Your party stops together when the quietest friend says it, so permission to pause does not belong only to the loudest hero.

quiet_rule_2_check.prompt: Agree that any friend may quietly call a pause. Choose who leads while the others help.

quiet_rule_2_done.narration: The whole group stops at the first signal, including Pip. The elder nods once and moves the cup away from the walking lane. You have a room rule everyone can use before there is anything surprising to look at.

quiet_rule_2_changed.narration: One friend cannot see the signal or hear the first quiet word. You change where the group stands and try the instruction facing one another. Everyone can repeat it before the elder leads you forward. Nothing in the old ice is tested by a shout.

witness_first.narration: The route worker gives the elder a drawing of the two valleys. Pip keeps your party's copy beside it. The elder does not begin by telling you what the memory means. She asks which parts were seen from the near bank, which from the far bank, and which were hidden by spray. The river outside has already changed again, so a good account needs its limits as well as its conclusion. How should your party start the comparison?

choices.label: Tell the sequence from each bank separately
Begin with the landmarks everyone could identify

witness_first_1.narration: You leave the pages side by side. The worker speaks from her own waiting place, and your party describes only the crossing it actually made. Pip points out where the views overlap. The elder keeps the separate accounts instead of turning them into a single confident voice.

witness_first_2.narration: You point out the chipped marker and two ridges on both pages. The worker confirms them before anyone describes the water. Pip marks the parts hidden by spray. The elder can now ask about a changed course without having to decide whether somebody named the wrong valley.

catalog_cards.narration: Three small catalog cards rest beside the ice. Each describes the same newly exposed memory from a different inspection. The elder says the yetis have re-cataloged it three times. Pip starts to arrange the cards as dates; she gently turns them sideways. The order of inspecting a memory is not the age of what it shows. Your party can preserve useful differences without making the cards into a timeline they cannot prove. How will you keep them together?

choices.label: Group them by the viewpoint each keeper recorded
Keep the inspection order and leave the memory undated

catalog_cards_1.narration: You look for the descriptions of ridge and river on each card. A friend reads the viewpoint aloud while another places the matching drawing beside it. The elder keeps the original cards separate. Your arrangement helps someone repeat a look rather than claiming when the river first changed.

catalog_cards_2.narration: You ask the elder to show which inspection happened first and copy only that sequence. Pip leaves a wide blank where a year might otherwise have gone. Each card still belongs to a visit, but no visit is mistaken for the date of the remembered scene.

listening_floor.narration: A faint low song travels through the floor from a hall elsewhere in the ice. The elder pauses to let your party feel it through still feet. It is not a command that makes a memory give up an answer. Yetis sing here while they work and keep their voices low. Pip asks whether he should hum along or stay silent. Your party can choose a respectful way to settle before reading without claiming to know an old song's missing words. What will you do?

choices.label: Listen through a full phrase before offering a quiet answer
Stay silent and follow the elder's slow approach

listening_floor_1.narration: You stand together until the low phrase ends. A songkeeper may help the party find a comfortable breath, but the elder invites everyone to listen. You offer one soft note only after there is space for it, leaving the old words unguessed.

listening_floor_2.narration: You let the song continue without adding to it. Pip closes his notebook while you cross the marked floor. The elder waits at each turn for the last friend. Silence becomes an active choice to make room for another people's work, not a test anyone can fail.

support_ice.narration: The memory face remains part of the glacier. A shallow wooden cradle below it catches loose surface flakes, keeping them off the place where visitors stand. One corner has settled into soft snow since the room was opened. The elder wants it supported before anyone leans close to the ice. There are sound wedges beside the cradle and room to reach from the marked floor. Your party can steady the corner or move the standing place farther back. Which arrangement will you try?

choices.label: Set the wedges while friends steady the cradle
Shift the viewing place back from the soft corner

support_ice_1.narration: You ask the elder which part of the wood can safely take pressure. One friend keeps the cradle from twisting while another slides a wedge from the marked floor. Pip stays back with the cards. No one pushes on the memory face to force an answer into view.

support_ice_1_check.prompt: Set the wedges while friends steady the cradle. Choose who leads while the others help.

support_ice_1_done.narration: The cradle and standing place stay steady under the elder's gentle test. She removes the loose snow around the wedges so the next visitor can see how the support works. Your party can begin looking without balancing on something that was never meant to bear it.

support_ice_1_changed.narration: The corner shifts before you finish. Everyone steps back to the marked floor while the elder supports it with a sound board. Your party helps move the standing place farther away. You will read from there, with the uncertain corner clearly marked out of bounds.

support_ice_2.narration: You move only the loose standing mat, leaving the ice and cradle where they are. The elder checks the sight line from the new place. A friend holds the mat flat while another marks its edge. You will accept a less convenient view if it keeps the room steady.

support_ice_2_check.prompt: Shift the viewing place back from the soft corner. Choose who leads while the others help.

support_ice_2_done.narration: The cradle and standing place stay steady under the elder's gentle test. She removes the loose snow around the wedges so the next visitor can see how the support works. Your party can begin looking without balancing on something that was never meant to bear it.

support_ice_2_changed.narration: The corner shifts before you finish. Everyone steps back to the marked floor while the elder supports it with a sound board. Your party helps move the standing place farther away. You will read from there, with the uncertain corner clearly marked out of bounds.

first_memory.narration: Within the pale ice, a small moving view becomes clear. Water leaves the glacier between two familiar ridges and runs down the valley that was dry on Pip's earlier drawing. No person in the remembered view names the river, and no date appears beside it. The elder asks the party to watch one complete passage before explaining. Your task is to notice what the ice actually shows, including what it does not show. How will you divide that first quiet look?

choices.label: Have different friends watch the river and the ridges
Have everyone follow one fixed landmark through the view

first_memory_1.narration: You ask Pip to keep the ridges in view while your party follows the water. The elder lets each observer finish before anyone compares accounts. Pip notes your words beside his own, including where each of you stood. Nobody gets to change an account just to make the sketches match.

first_memory_2.narration: Your party agrees on the fork-shaped ridge before the next moving passage. Each friend watches where the water leaves beside it. Pip compares the accounts when the view has passed. Nobody fills the blank beyond the remembered valley with an imagined map of the whole realm.

second_view.narration: The elder leads you to a second marked viewpoint, still on the safe floor. A cloudy layer inside the ice partly overlaps the remembered river. From here, a reflection could make a bend seem to run in another direction. Your party has one drawing from outside and one first account from the memory face. Before deciding that they agree, you can check the fixed ridges again or compare the order in which the water passes visible rocks. Which check would challenge your first impression?

choices.label: Keep the ridges fixed while comparing both views
Trace the passage past three visible rocks
Compare the two observers' separate notes

second_view_1.narration: You leave Pip's outside sketch upright and ask a friend to point to the matching shapes in the ice. The elder marks where you stood for the first look. You compare one bend at a time, refusing to rotate the drawing simply to make the river agree.

second_view_1_check.prompt: Keep the ridges fixed while comparing both views. Choose who leads while the others help.

second_view_1_done.narration: The two ridge profiles agree from both safe viewpoints. Holding the sketch upright makes the reflection slide away from their fixed edges. Your own observers can point to the match without the elder choosing the bend for them. Pip marks the two places you stood, leaving the memory's age and cause blank.

second_view_1_changed.narration: The reflection hides the middle bend. Your party leaves it blank. With the elder's side view you can see the river leave by the other valley, but you did not independently check the obscured part. She offers to co-read the account if you want to cite that direction. Pip keeps the difference between your observations and her help visible.

second_view_2.narration: You choose three rocks that stay in view and have separate friends watch them. Pip notes their order only after the passage ends. The elder waits beside the safe mark while your party checks whether a bright reflection could reverse any part of the sequence.

second_view_2_check.prompt: Trace the passage past three visible rocks. Choose who leads while the others help.

second_view_2_done.narration: Your observers record the three rocks in order as the remembered water passes them. The same sequence appears from the second viewpoint, while a reflection moves the other way. Pip numbers the observation positions on your sketch, not the years. Your party can cite a checked sequence rather than just a matching silhouette.

second_view_2_changed.narration: The reflection hides the middle bend. Your party leaves it blank. With the elder's side view you can see the river leave by the other valley, but you did not independently check the obscured part. She offers to co-read the account if you want to cite that direction. Pip keeps the difference between your observations and her help visible.

what_matches.narration: The outside drawing and the memory account lie together on the elder's stone table. Your party watched the river briefly take that valley today; the ice preserves a view of it leaving there at another time. The elder asks which agreement is solid and which questions remain open. Neither page tells you why land has been moving. Pip leaves his pencil on the table so the next sentence is chosen by the party rather than by the person holding the pencil. Which agreement should lead the note?

choices.label: Cite the direction your own observers checked
Lead with the limits of the match
Ask the elder to co-read and sign the direction

variants.text: The elder waits for your observers to choose whether to put their own checked direction in the account.
Your middle bend is still blank. The elder can sign a co-reading, or you can keep the account limited to the visible landmarks.

what_matches_1.narration: You place the independently checked direction in the account, with the age and cause left open. The elder asks the observers to point out their evidence before she lets Pip copy the sentence. They can show how they checked it, rather than asking the next reader to trust a confident voice.

variants.text: Your three-rock sequence is the evidence you cite. Pip keeps the order of the rocks beside the direction.
Your two ridge profiles and standing positions are the evidence you cite. Pip keeps both viewpoints beside the direction.

what_matches_2.narration: You state that the ice shows one local river view, while your party saw only a brief change outside. The shared landmarks make the comparison useful. The elder adds the confirmed direction beneath the limits, so uncertainty does not erase the observation and confidence does not grow beyond it.

catalog_test.narration: A younger yeti keeper brings a fresh catalog slip and asks where the new account belongs. She can file it with the outside crossing report, with the memory's earlier inspections, or cross-reference both. A wrong place would not destroy the memory, but could make the next visitor miss half the evidence. The elder asks your party to find one clear route through the records from a question someone might really bring. Where should the younger keeper begin the test?

choices.label: Begin with a visitor asking about the changed crossing
Begin with a visitor asking about the old river view

variants.text: The younger keeper must be able to find both of your standing positions from the ridge-profile account.
She is testing whether another reader can reach your cited evidence without your party pointing to it.
The elder supplies her signed cross-reference for the co-reading. You may use it to make the keeper's first filing test easier.

catalog_test_1.narration: You hand the keeper the outside sketch and ask her to find the memory view that can be compared with it. Pip stays quiet while she follows the references. Your party watches where a label sends her toward an inspection date instead of the remembered river.

catalog_test_1_check.prompt: Begin with a visitor asking about the changed crossing. Choose who leads while the others help.

catalog_test_1_done.narration: The younger keeper follows the cards to both accounts without a keeper guiding her. She can distinguish the outside crossing from the undated memory and point to the evidence the account names. She offers to post a visitor guide if your party wants to share one. A later reader could follow this route without waiting for a keeper.

catalog_test_1_changed.narration: The younger keeper mistakes the inspection order for the river's age. You correct the label together, but she still needs the elder to show where the account meets the ice. "I will sit with the next reader," she says. A shared copy can be kept under a keeper's guidance; a guide for visitors to use alone needs another independent test.

catalog_test_2.narration: You hand the keeper the memory description and ask whether it leads her to today's outside witnesses. The worker stands ready to identify her own account. Your party checks that the path reaches a real observation instead of ending with a confident but unexplained copied sentence.

catalog_test_2_check.prompt: Begin with a visitor asking about the old river view. Choose who leads while the others help.

catalog_test_2_done.narration: The younger keeper follows the cards to both accounts without a keeper guiding her. She can distinguish the outside crossing from the undated memory and point to the evidence the account names. She offers to post a visitor guide if your party wants to share one. A later reader could follow this route without waiting for a keeper.

catalog_test_2_changed.narration: The younger keeper mistakes the inspection order for the river's age. You correct the label together, but she still needs the elder to show where the account meets the ice. "I will sit with the next reader," she says. A shared copy can be kept under a keeper's guidance; a guide for visitors to use alone needs another independent test.

sliding_tray.narration: While the younger keeper puts the catalog slip away, a shallow tray begins sliding on a patch of meltwater beside the work table. It holds spare blank slips and a little chalk, not a piece of memory ice. The tray is still on the safe side of the marked floor. Nobody needs to run toward the old wall or shout. Your party can stop its path or lift the papers from above. Which small rescue will leave the standing area clear?

choices.label: Catch the tray against the table from the safe side
Lift the slips while a friend blocks the tray's path
Use a wing as a barrier beside the marked floor

sliding_tray_1.narration: You keep your feet on the marked floor and ask Pip to move the loose stool out of the way. A friend reaches for the tray's near rim while another watches the meltwater patch. The elder stays between your party and the old ice, making the stopping point plain.

sliding_tray_1_check.prompt: Catch the tray against the table from the safe side. Choose who leads while the others help.

sliding_tray_1_done.narration: The slips and chalk return to the table without anyone leaving the safe floor. The younger keeper dries the tray and marks the meltwater patch. Pip checks the record pages one more time, then laughs softly at how carefully everyone is keeping even the blank paper.

sliding_tray_1_changed.narration: The tray bumps the table before you catch it. Two blank slips become wet, so the younger keeper sets them aside to dry. The written accounts stay on the upper stone. Your party moves the tray away from the meltwater and keeps the warning boundary where it was.

sliding_tray_2.narration: You leave the sliding tray low and reach for the dry slips first. Pip brings the empty cloth used to wrap the outside drawing. Another friend stops the tray from turning toward the walking lane. No one tries to catch a falling sheet by crossing the boundary.

sliding_tray_2_check.prompt: Lift the slips while a friend blocks the tray's path. Choose who leads while the others help.

sliding_tray_2_done.narration: The slips and chalk return to the table without anyone leaving the safe floor. The younger keeper dries the tray and marks the meltwater patch. Pip checks the record pages one more time, then laughs softly at how carefully everyone is keeping even the blank paper.

sliding_tray_2_changed.narration: The tray bumps the table before you catch it. Two blank slips become wet, so the younger keeper sets them aside to dry. The written accounts stay on the upper stone. Your party moves the tray away from the meltwater and keeps the warning boundary where it was.

compare_accounts.narration: The elder asks whether your party has another checked observation of a river where today's geography does not fit it. An earlier record could help, but nobody needs to invent one to complete this visit. The new memory already gives you a local clue: a river once left by a different valley. Pip separates the space for a comparison from the space for the observation itself. How will you handle what you know beyond this room?

choices.label: Compare only observations that can be pointed out
Ask the elder to keep the new clue on its own page

variants.text: At the Saltrot's buried bridge, your party recorded a waterline and rounded river pebbles beneath dry arches. That is a separate checked clue about water that no longer flows there; it does not prove both changes happened together.

compare_accounts_1.narration: You name the ridge, course and view that someone else can check. If another place is in your notes, you keep its own evidence beside its own name. The elder leaves a blank where no comparison has been made. A blank is more useful than a borrowed certainty.

compare_accounts_2.narration: You preserve the local river view without making it explain every strange thing your party has seen. Pip marks where another checked account could be added later. The elder agrees to compare the pages when they exist, not to fill the space with a theory today.

claim_limit.narration: Before the younger keeper copies the final sentence, the elder asks what it must not claim. A remembered river course does not name who changed it, and today's crossing does not date the ice. Pip suggests writing those limits beside the clue so the next traveler does not inherit a larger story than the party actually found. You can choose the question that should remain open most clearly, while leaving the others open too. Which limit should be easiest to spot?

claim_limit_1.narration: You put the confirmed course first, followed by a short statement that its cause is not known. The worker adds her account of today's return to the older bed separately. Nobody gives the ice a voice naming a culprit, and no blank becomes an excuse to accuse a neighbor.

claim_limit_2.narration: You put the matched landmarks first and leave the memory without a year. The younger keeper lists the three inspection visits on another line. A reader can now distinguish the age of an observation from the time at which someone wrote it down.

record_choice.narration: The elder offers to keep a copy of your party's finished comparison beside the memory catalog. You may also keep your own drawing without carrying ice or taking an object from the room. A shared copy could help later visitors check the same view; a private page lets you choose when to explain your work. The elder will keep the original memory safe either way. What would your party like her to do with its own written account?

choices.label: Leave a checked copy for future visitors
Keep the party's page without adding it to the catalog
Publish the independently tested visitor guide
Leave a keeper-guided copy with its limits marked

variants.text: Your filing path passed an independent test. You may also publish a guide that lets visitors find the view without waiting for a keeper.
The corrected filing path still needs a keeper. If you share a copy, the younger keeper will guide its next reader; it will not be posted as a guide for use alone.

record_choice_1.narration: You compare the elder's copy with the page your party keeps. Both show the confirmed local course and the unanswered questions. Pip reads back the parts hidden by glare or spray. The younger keeper files your copy only after every hero has had a chance to correct it.

record_choice_2.narration: You thank the elder for the viewing and keep your finished page together with the outside account. She accepts that the words are yours to share. The younger keeper files the room's own observations without claiming your party gave permission to copy its whole account.

teach_back.narration: An arriving yeti visitor waits at the warm cup, just as your party did. The elder asks whether you would like to explain the safe view while she watches. This is a chance to find a confusing instruction before the next reading. The visitor has seen neither the crossing nor the memory and does not know Pip's drawing. Your party must give enough guidance to look, without handing over a grand history the ice has not shown. How will you begin?

choices.label: Start with the quiet rule and fixed landmarks
Ask the visitor to separate a view from an explanation

variants.text: The newcomer finds your posted guide and reaches the safe standing mark before the keeper needs to lead them. The younger keeper lets your party see that it works for someone new.
The younger keeper brings the newcomer from her seat with the assisted copy. Your earlier filing difficulty is now part of her instructions, not silently erased.
Your private account stays with your party. The elder uses the room's own observations for the newcomer and asks you only to demonstrate a safe way to look.
Pip asks the newcomer to find the evidence your observers cited before accepting the direction. Your party's own check remains visible in the lesson.

teach_back_1.narration: You show where to stand and how to call a pause. Then you let the visitor find the two ridges before describing the water. Pip keeps the map steady instead of pointing to a conclusion. The elder waits to hear the visitor's own account of what becomes visible.

teach_back_1_check.prompt: Start with the quiet rule and fixed landmarks. Choose who leads while the others help.

teach_back_1_done.narration: The visitor describes a river leaving by the other valley and asks when it happened. Your party answers that the view does not give a date. The elder nods. A useful clue has been passed on without turning one fragment into the history of the whole glacier.

teach_back_1_changed.narration: The visitor first repeats your words rather than describing the ice. You step back and let the elder give them a longer quiet look. Their next account names the ridges and water separately. Your party corrects its introduction so another reader can make an observation of their own.

teach_back_2.narration: You give the visitor the safe standing place and ask what can actually be seen there. Your party listens before comparing it with today's crossing. Pip keeps the undated memory and the inspected route on separate pages. The elder is ready to correct any instruction that invites a shout.

teach_back_2_check.prompt: Ask the visitor to separate a view from an explanation. Choose who leads while the others help.

teach_back_2_done.narration: The visitor describes a river leaving by the other valley and asks when it happened. Your party answers that the view does not give a date. The elder nods. A useful clue has been passed on without turning one fragment into the history of the whole glacier.

teach_back_2_changed.narration: The visitor first repeats your words rather than describing the ice. You step back and let the elder give them a longer quiet look. Their next account names the ridges and water separately. Your party corrects its introduction so another reader can make an observation of their own.

rest.narration: The ice has shown a river leaving the glacier by the other valley, matching the brief course your party witnessed outside. Its age and cause remain unanswered. You keep a drawing and a checked observation, not a piece of the glacier or a complete old map. The elder repeats her warning about the old ice without naming what might wake. Pip closes the pages carefully. The party can return to the workers by the upper path or pause here before following the next part of the northern strand.

variants.text: Behind you, the posted guide lets another visitor find the memory without waiting for a keeper. The younger keeper credits your party for the usable route.
The keeper keeps the copy you chose to share. It remains an account for discussion, not a posted guide claiming that a reader can work alone.
No copy of your private account is filed. The elder accepts your decision and keeps her own observations separate.

quiet_rule_assisted.narration: A songkeeper helps the party practice the quiet pause at a comfortable breath. The elder listens from the marked floor and gives the least confident friend room to call it. Another hero can lead the check of whether everyone understood. The song does not command the old ice.

quiet_rule_assisted_check.prompt: Let a songkeeper lead a quiet pause signal. The qualified hero assists; choose who leads the team check.

sliding_tray_assisted.narration: A winged friend holds a broad wing beside the safe walking space to keep blank slips from drifting toward the boundary. Your party stays on the floor, not in flight among the ice shelves. The most nimble helper can collect the tray while the wing supplies a quiet barrier.

sliding_tray_assisted_check.prompt: Use a wing as a barrier beside the marked floor. The qualified hero assists; choose who leads the team check.

second_view_prepared.narration: Your two observers open their separate accounts. One followed the water; the other kept the ridges fixed. You compare the accounts before Pip lays the outside sketch beside them. The elder asks the observers to point out their own positions. A prepared comparison can challenge the reflection without asking one witness to remember everything.

second_view_prepared_check.prompt: Use the two independent accounts to check the reflected river view.

what_matches_keeper.narration: You ask the elder to co-read the direction and put her name beside it. She follows the visible course from a clear side view, then signs only that part of the account. Your own observations stay separately marked. A later reader can ask the keeper about her contribution rather than treating either a respected name or your party's confidence as the whole proof.

variants.text: Your middle bend remains blank; the signed direction comes from the elder's side view, not an observation you secretly completed.
Although your independent check succeeded, you choose to make this a co-reading. Your own evidence is retained, and the keeper takes responsibility for her separate contribution.

catalog_endorsed.narration: You give the younger keeper the elder's signed reference and ask her to follow it before anyone adds instructions. The signature identifies the co-reader; it does not supply a date. Your party can test whether the reference leads to the view and its limits, rather than treating a respected name as an answer.

catalog_endorsed_check.prompt: Test the signed cross-reference without guiding the new reader.

record_publish.narration: You give permission to post the checked account and its route through the catalog. Pip copies the limits beside the view, not on a separate sheet someone might miss. The younger keeper puts the guide where arriving visitors can find it. Your party has changed how the next reader can use the room, without handing out a complete history.

record_staff_copy.narration: You leave a copy that clearly marks where a keeper must help. The younger keeper puts it beside her seat instead of posting it as a self-service guide. She agrees to explain the corrected date label to the next visitor. Your party has chosen a useful assisted record rather than hiding the failed test.

voiceGuide.tone: Warm, funny, curious, with real consequences. Describe actions and sensory details directly. Short dialogue. Never use "the kind of thing that", "the sort of thing that", or "it was X, the type of thing that makes you Y" comparisons. Let a character act instead of explaining how the reader should feel.
voiceGuide.vocabulary: Read aloud to an eight-year-old. Concrete words, short sentences, distinct voices.

npcVoices.Pip Thistledown: Manticore scout. Eager but learns to separate observation from guess; never knows an unseen event.
npcVoices.Yeti keepers: Slow, enormous and gentle. Deliberate before answering. Offer a safe method and leave unknown history unknown.
